Dwarf Planet. A dwarf planet is a celestial body that orbits the Sun, possesses sufficient mass to achieve hydrostatic equilibrium—a round shape—but has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of other debris. The category was created in two thousand six by the International Astronomical Union. Pluto, once the ninth planet, was famously reclassified as a dwarf planet, alongside Ceres and other icy bodies, fundamentally altering the Solar System's taxonomy and igniting ongoing debate among astronomers.

The IAU definition of a planet requires three conditions. It must orbit the Sun, possess enough mass to be round, and have cleared the neighborhood around its orbit of other objects—removing gravitational competitors.

Dwarf planets satisfy the first two criteria but fail the third. They orbit in regions with other similar bodies, such as Kuiper Belt objects and asteroids, and have not achieved gravitational dominance.

Pluto was reclassified from planet to dwarf planet in two thousand six. It shares its orbital region, the Kuiper Belt, with thousands of similar-sized or larger icy bodies, violating the neighborhood-clearing requirement.

Ceres, the largest asteroid in the asteroid belt, was also reclassified from asteroid to dwarf planet in two thousand six under the same decision. It comprises about one-third of the asteroid belt's total mass.

Other recognized dwarf planets include Haumea, Makemake, and Eris. Eris is more distant than Pluto and more massive, with highly elliptical orbits. Dozens more dwarf planets are suspected and await confirmation.

Eris was discovered in two thousand five and prompted the IAU's reclassification debate. Its discovery showed that Pluto was not unique and that many Kuiper Belt objects were comparable in size, making "planet" scientifically ambiguous.

Dwarf planets are scientifically interesting as preserved remnants of the Solar System's formation. Their compositions and orbits reveal the conditions in the protoplanetary disk and the history of gravitational interactions among early solar system bodies.
